prompt.context: Your firm has won an RFP to help a domestic airline carrier examine their in-flight connectivity (IFC) strategy. With 80% of US-based aircraft already outfitted with IFC technology and competitive pressures rising, offering WiFi service is becoming table-stakes. Your client has yet to enter the game, but they know it's something they need to consider to stay competitive.
prompt.question: What are some of the key things the client should think about when assessing their go-to-market strategy for IFC?

clarifying_info.q: What routes does the airline fly?
clarifying_info.a: Primarily domestic routes within the continental US, as well as select flights to Canada, Mexico, and the Caribbean.
IFC includes only WiFi connectivity. In-flight entertainment (IFE) is delivered via an on-board server through a separate system, but the two can be integrated into one user experience.

clarifying_info.q: What is the airline's main objective?
clarifying_info.a: The airline's main objective is to stay competitive.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the airline's fleet and how many flights does it operate?
clarifying_info.a: The airline has 90 planes and services approximately 30,000 flights per year.

clarifying_info.q: Who typically installs and manages IFC?
clarifying_info.a: IFC is typically installed and managed by an outside vendor, either through a branded service (e.g., GoGoAir) or a wholesale, white-label solution (e.g., Row44). Contracts are typically 10+ years long.

clarifying_info.q: Do all vendors use the same technology?
clarifying_info.a: Different vendors use different technologies, which vary in quality.

clarifying_info.q: How does bandwidth work across passengers?
clarifying_info.a: Total bandwidth is shared across passengers, so the more passengers buy a session, the slower the service. Some carriers intentionally charge high prices to limit usage and ensure better service.

framework: ROI and/or profitability: determine whether IFC can generate sufficient returns given upfront investment and ongoing costs
Pricing and pricing model: evaluate options such as free, ad-supported, pay per data usage, pay per time, pay by speed tier, or subscription service
Market demand: assess take rate expectations and segment demand (business vs. leisure, cabin class, flight length)
Costs: quantify upfront capital investment and ongoing operating costs
Vendor contract structure: understand revenue/business model, split of investment costs and OpEx, branding rights, contract length, and technology quality
Product/user experience: consider built-in screens vs. BYO-device, white-label vs. vendor-branding, speeds available, interoperability with IFE, add-on services (calling, texting)
Technology: evaluate speed, bandwidth, latency, and availability over water
GTM strategy: plan rollout timing, marketing approach, crew training, and potential ad sales

questions.prompt: Question 1: Your analyst pulled benchmarks on what two competitors are doing today. What are your thoughts on these two models? [Exhibit 1]
questions.guidance:
Candidate should analyze pros and cons of each model and recognize these are not the only two options. Strong candidates will consider elements beyond those listed in the exhibit (e.g., cost structure, technology quality, interoperability with IFE).

Competitor 1 (vendor-branded, revenue share, $25/session):
- Pros: less operational burden on airline, potential for customer experience continuity (e.g., cross-carrier subscriptions), limited upfront costs
- Cons: limited control over pricing (high price could drive low take rates and anger customers), brand fit considerations

Competitor 2 (airline-branded, wholesale, free):
- Pros: full control over pricing, full control over user experience, potential for better ROI, easier integration with airline's other products (e.g., IFE system)
- Cons: more operational burden on airline, higher costs

Other considerations: who funds the initial investment, ongoing cost structure, potential to adopt more than one model across different fleet segments, technology limitations (vendors are not equal). Clarification: one session = WiFi connectivity for the duration of the flight.

questions.prompt: Question 2: The client has decided to partner with a white-label IFC vendor to outfit all 90 planes. The airline and vendor will share the initial investment, and then the airline will pay the vendor a per-session fee to cover operating expenses. What percentage of passengers need to purchase a session for the airline to break even in 2 years? [Exhibit 2]
questions.guidance:
Strong candidate will set up the break-even equation cleanly, arrive at ~12.9%, and then react to the result — noting it exceeds current industry take rates of 5-10% and discussing implications.

Advanced candidates will proactively flag assumptions: 100% seat occupancy rate and simultaneous outfitting of all aircraft may be optimistic.

Capex and margin data should be given only when the candidate specifically asks:
- Capex = $250K per plane; airline covers 40%
- Margin = $10 per session (ad revenues already baked in)

Assumptions given by casebook: seat occupancy rate = 100%, all aircraft outfitted at the same time, ad revenues baked into margin, 1 WiFi session covers entire flight.

math.setup: Break-even: Total passengers over 2 years x take rate x $10/session = Total airline investment
steps: Wide body passengers (2 yrs) = 300 seats x 2,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 1,500,000
Narrow body passengers (2 yrs) = 100 seats x 27,500 flights/yr x 2 yrs = 5,500,000
math.answer: Required take rate ≈ 12.9%. This exceeds current industry take rates of 5-10%, indicating break-even in 2 years is ambitious.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Market research tells us that take rates are only between 5 and 10% today for paid connectivity, so the client is concerned about hitting break-even targets. What do you think are the key drivers of IFC take rate?
questions.guidance:
This is a correlation question: what variables are correlated with higher take rates? Candidate should brainstorm broadly and hypothesize the direction each variable would need to swing to drive higher take rate.

Flight characteristics: flight length (longer = higher), flight time (daytime > red-eye), availability of other entertainment systems (lower IFE quality = higher take rate)
Product characteristics: price (lower = higher), speeds available (faster = higher), quality of service (better = higher), number of connected devices allowed (more = higher)
Passenger characteristics: age (younger = higher), income (higher = higher), cabin class (business/first = higher), trip type (business travel = higher)

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key drivers of IFC take rate? Brainstorm as many variables as possible and indicate which direction each must swing to drive a higher take rate.

categories.name: Flight characteristics
ideas: Flight length — longer flights correlate with higher take rates
Flight time — daytime flights have higher take rates than red-eyes
Availability of other entertainment — lower IFE quality increases WiFi take rate

categories.name: Product characteristics
ideas: Price — lower price drives higher take rate
Speeds available — faster speeds drive higher take rate
Quality of service — better reliability drives higher take rate
Number of connected devices allowed — allowing more devices drives higher take rate

categories.name: Passenger characteristics
ideas: Age — younger passengers have higher take rates
Income level — higher-income passengers have higher take rates
Cabin class — business/first class passengers have higher take rates
Trip purpose — business travelers have higher take rates than leisure travelers

recommendation: The airline should partner with a wholesale, white-label vendor to retain full control over pricing and the user experience
Roll-out across the fleet should be gradual, with a potential pilot program to optimize pricing and user experience before full deployment
Roll-out should prioritize newer planes covering routes with high expected take rates (e.g., longer routes with higher share of business travelers)
risks: Due to the large upfront investment, the contract is likely to be 10+ years long, making smart vendor selection extremely critical
Difficult to strike the right balance between maximizing revenue and maintaining a sufficiently low take rate to ensure higher speeds for connected passengers
Technology is still nascent — there is potential for poor user experience that could damage the brand
next_steps: Aircraft prioritization — identify routes and planes with highest expected take rates for first-wave deployment
Pilot launch to test pricing, user experience, and demand before full fleet rollout
